title: Philadelphia museum closes despite campaign and temporary funding offer
summary:
Philadelphia's Academy of Natural Sciences Museum has closed to the public, leaving families and supporters asking whether a major place for learning about nature can reopen. The closure was announced on September 1, with September 30 set as its final day.

Families made farewell visits throughout the month. For many, the museum had been part of childhood across several generations. Alexandria McCormick, visiting with her husband and six children, said her own visits had helped awaken her love of natural history.

Founded in 1812 and opened to the public in 1828, the Academy became the first place in the world to display a dinosaur skeleton in 1868. It also offered mammal displays, live animals and changing exhibitions.

Drexel University, which took financial responsibility for the Academy in 2011, says costs rose and attendance fell after the pandemic. Drexel has also faced financial difficulties connected partly to declining enrollment. The museum cut staff and hours in 2025 and later cancelled its 2026 summer camp.

Supporters organized rallies and a petition with more than 114,000 signatures. Some criticized the short notice and questioned whether enough had been done to prevent closure. Attendance surged during the final weeks, with revenue more than 20 times higher than the previous September.

Less than a week before closing, the William Penn Foundation offered a year of bridge funding. That means temporary financial support while a longer-term solution is explored. Drexel says it is considering working with the foundation, but would require a plan for lasting financial stability before considering reopening.

Philadelphia's city council plans public hearings to investigate the decision and possible solutions. It also proposed changing local land-use rules to make selling the building or converting it to other uses more difficult.

The Academy's collection contains more than 19 million specimens, including plant samples gathered by Lewis and Clark. Its 73,000 holotype specimens serve as scientific references for defining and naming species. Drexel says students and researchers will retain collection access, but what access the general public will have remains uncertain.
why_it_matters: The closure affects families' access to nature education and a major scientific collection. Temporary funding and public hearings could help explore solutions, but reopening is uncertain.
